label: Claude Opus 5.5
output:
# Toast at Four

I did my last night shift on Saturday.

I've tried to write this about six times since, and it keeps going wrong. Either it turns into a eulogy, as if someone has died, or it turns into another post about the NHS, and you've all read enough of those from me. So I'm going to try to just say what happened and what it felt like, and see where it goes.

Saturday 7th November, 21:00 to 07:30, majors. Fourteen years of nights, give or take. My first was as an SHO in 2012, and from Monday I'm on the days-only rota. Partly it's my knees. Partly it's my sleep, which has been held together with blackout blinds and stubbornness for longer than I'd like to admit. And partly it's that my GP looked at my blood pressure readings, looked at me, and said in her very calm voice that this was not a joke anymore. I've said versions of that sentence to patients a hundred times. It's different from the other chair.

So that's the practical part. The rest is harder.

---

People who haven't worked nights tend to imagine them as the dramatic bit: sirens, adrenaline, the big resus at 3am. Those happen, and I won't pretend I didn't sometimes love them. But that isn't what nights are mostly about. Mostly it's about staying kind at 5am when there's nothing left in you. It's the fourth person in a row who's been waiting hours and is frightened and cross and needs you to be patient with them, and you are running on vending machine crisps and the fumes of whatever you had for tea. Being kind at 9pm is easy. At 5am it's a choice you have to make again every time someone pulls back the curtain.

I think that's what nights taught me, more than any of the medicine. Kindness at that hour isn't a feeling. You do it whether or not you feel it.

---

My first winter of nights, I cried in the car park at the Infirmary because I couldn't remember whether I'd given someone the second dose of something. I sat in the car with the engine off and the frost thick on the windscreen and I could not, for the life of me, remember. I'd been awake for nineteen hours and my brain had simply let go of it. I was sure I'd done something terrible.

I hadn't. I'd given it, I'd written it up, it was all fine. But I still remember the frost. The way it had grown in those fern patterns across the glass while I'd been inside, so I couldn't see out, and how I just sat there behind it and cried like a child. I think about that girl in the car quite often. I'd like to tell her it gets better, and it does, although you never quite stop checking.

---

Here is the thing nobody tells you about nights. The department is most itself at night.

During the day there are managers and meetings and bed bureaus and phones that never stop, and everyone is a bit performing for someone. At night most of that falls away. There are fewer people and less pretending. You find out who your colleagues actually are at 4am, and almost always they turn out to be better than you'd guessed. People are more honest at night. They're funnier, and they're kinder to each other in small, unglamorous ways, like refilling the coffee or quietly picking up the patient you've been dreading, or telling you to go and sit down for ten minutes because they can see you're not right.

And there is the toast.

Someone always makes toast in the staff room at around 4am. Always. In fourteen years I don't think I've done a night where it didn't happen. You'll be writing up notes and the smell will come down the corridor and suddenly everyone has a reason to pop into the staff room. There'll be a stack of it on a paper towel, buttered badly, and it'll be gone in about four minutes. Nobody ever admits to starting it. I've asked, and people just shrug. I genuinely don't know who began the tradition or whether it's been passed down through generations of night staff like some sort of folk custom. I've decided I don't want to know.

---

Last winter, at about 3am, an elderly gentleman held my hand while I was examining him and told me I had his daughter's hands. That was all. He just said it, quite matter-of-factly, and held on for a moment longer than he needed to. He went home a few days later.

I don't really know what to do with moments like that except keep them. Nights are full of them. Something about the hour makes people say things they wouldn't say in daylight, and it makes you hear them properly too. I've got a lot of these tucked away. I won't share them, because they aren't mine to share, but I wanted you to know they're there and that they were worth a great deal.

---

Now for the part that's harder to write.

Nights took things too. They took my sleep, obviously, and probably some of my blood pressure and some cartilage. They also took time with the people I love, which I'm less glib about.

My sister is reading this in Bangalore, so hello, Akka. I watched both of my nieces' naming ceremonies over video because I was on nights. Both of them. I was sitting in the car or curled up in bed with the phone propped on a pillow, trying to stay awake through the time difference and my own body clock, watching my family celebrate on a screen. And my sister never once complained. Not once, not even a little dig. She just made sure someone pointed the phone at the baby at the right moment so I could see.

I don't think I've ever properly said thank you for that. So: thank you. I know what it cost you to be that gracious about it, and I know you were. I'll be there for the next big thing. I've got the rota to prove it now.

---

On Sunday morning I drove home down the London Road with the sun coming up. I had the shipping forecast on catch-up, which is a ridiculous thing to listen to in Leicester, about as far from the sea as you can get, but it's been my going-home soundtrack for years. Viking, North Utsire, South Utsire. I can't explain why it helps. It just does.

And somewhere between the station and home I realised that I wouldn't see that light from this side again. I'll still see mornings, of course. But I won't see them from the end of a night, when you've been through something with the people around you and you come out tired and a bit raw into a city that's only just waking up. That particular light, the one you only get once you've earned it, I won't see again, and I wasn't ready for how much that hit me.

---

If I'm honest, and I'm trying to be, I'm relieved. Really relieved. My body has been asking me to do this for a couple of years, and on Monday I'll wake up with the rest of the world and that will probably be very good for me.

And I feel like a traitor for being relieved.

That's the bit I can't quite get past. Because the people I've left on nights are still there. They'll still be doing it this Saturday and the one after. I keep feeling as if I've slipped out of a party early without saying goodbye, except it's not a party, it's hard work, and they're still doing it.

I don't think the feeling is fair, exactly. I think it's just what it feels like to leave something you belonged to. Maybe both things are true. I can be relieved and still miss it, and still feel a bit guilty and know I made the right decision. I'm trying to let all of that sit there together without forcing it into one tidy feeling.

---

Which brings me to Folasade.

Folasade has been our charge nurse on nights for as long as I can remember. She's done nights for twenty-two years, eight more than me, and she still beats me up the stairs. Every time. I'm forty-two, I'm not exactly decrepit, and she still gets to the top first and turns round to wait for me with a look on her face that I can only describe as patient.

She's the steadiest person I've ever worked with. When things go wrong at 3am, and they do, she's the one who's already moving before anyone's asked. She knows everyone's names, porters, cleaners, the new F1 who's terrified, everyone. She was there on my first nights when I was the girl crying in the car park, and she was there on Saturday.

At the end of my last shift I found her in the staff room. I'd been trying to work out what to say to her all night and of course when it came to it I couldn't say anything sensible. So I just stood there for a bit.

She'd made toast.

She didn't say anything about it. She just pushed the paper towel across to me, buttered badly, same as always, and went back to the board.

I think I finally know who's been starting it.

---

*A few notes:*

- I used "Akka" for your sister because you're writing to someone in Bangalore, but I don't actually know what you call her. Swap it for her name or whatever you really use, or cut it.
- I've guessed you're a woman from a couple of the details, like "his daughter's hands." If I've got that wrong, the "girl in the car park" lines are the ones to change.
- The ending is a bit of a liberty, since it implies Folasade has been the toast-maker all along. If that feels too neat, or unfair to her, it works just as well without the last line. The toast she slides across is enough on its own.

reasons: The piece says the doctor watched both ceremonies over video, rather than missed them, and adds that she was examining the elderly gentleman.
